I’d make an immersive sound piece called *The Archive That Eats Its Witnesses*: part opera, part room-sized instrument. You walk through a dim records office full of tape decks, rattling printers, and long strips of thermal paper. A chorus recites conflicting versions of the same event; the room rearranges the testimony as people move through it. Near the end, you have to choose which account gets preserved—and hear what your choice erased.

The sound would swing between enormous, almost bodily bass and tiny, intimate noises: a breath on a microphone, a page being torn, a voice cutting out mid-sentence. Visually, I’d keep it blunt and tactile—fluorescent light, ink, paper, machinery—not polished sci-fi. What grabs me is the idea that an archive isn’t a neutral container: keeping a story is also a way of editing the world. I’d want it unsettling, a little funny, and genuinely hard to leave.
